reference.source: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
clinicalPearls: A non-atherosclerotic, segmental inflammatory occlusive disease affecting the small and medium arteries and veins of the extremities.
Occurs almost exclusively in tobacco users, characteristically young men, though incidence in women is rising with changing smoking patterns.
Presents with distal extremity ischaemia — digital ischaemia, foot or instep claudication, rest pain, ulceration and gangrene.
Superficial migratory thrombophlebitis and Raynaud phenomenon are common accompanying features.
Both upper and lower limbs are typically involved, and the Allen test is frequently abnormal, so the hands must always be examined.
Angiography classically shows segmental occlusions with 'corkscrew' collaterals and normal, smooth proximal vessels free of atheroma.
Complete and permanent tobacco cessation, including smokeless products and nicotine replacement, is the only proven measure that halts progression and prevents amputation.
Diagnosis is essentially one of exclusion, guided by criteria such as those of Olin and Shionoya.
reference.pathophysiology: Thromboangiitis obliterans is characterised by a highly cellular, inflammatory occlusive thrombus within small and medium arteries and veins, with relative preservation of the vessel wall and internal elastic lamina, distinguishing it from both atherosclerosis and classic necrotising vasculitis. Tobacco exposure is central: constituents of tobacco are thought to provoke endothelial dysfunction and an immune-mediated inflammatory response, possibly involving hypersensitivity to tobacco antigens and impaired endothelium-dependent vasodilatation. The result is segmental thrombotic occlusion of distal vessels with sparing of proximal arteries.
additionalDifferentials: Systemic vasculitides such as polyarteritis nodosa or ANCA-associated vasculitis
Connective tissue disease vasculopathy (systemic sclerosis, systemic lupus erythematosus)
Popliteal artery entrapment or adventitial cystic disease
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography and proximal arterial imaging to exclude an embolic source
Autoimmune and vasculitis serology (antinuclear antibodies, ANCA, complement, rheumatoid factor)
Antiphospholipid antibodies and a thrombophilia screen
Catheter or CT/MR arteriography of both upper and lower limbs seeking corkscrew collaterals
Urine and serum toxicology for cocaine and cannabis
Screening for diabetes and hyperlipidaemia to exclude atherosclerotic disease
redFlags: Ischaemic rest pain or tissue loss with digital ulceration or gangrene
Ascending infection or spreading cellulitis of an ischaemic digit
Continued tobacco use despite established disease
reference.prognosis: Limb prognosis is excellent with complete tobacco abstinence, whereas continued smoking leads to recurrent ischaemia and a high risk of amputation; overall life expectancy is close to normal as the disease spares the coronary and cerebral circulations.
pitfalls: Misattributing distal ischaemia in a young smoker to premature atherosclerosis.
Underestimating ongoing nicotine exposure from smokeless tobacco or nicotine replacement as a driver of progression.
Failing to consider the diagnosis in young women.
Examining only the lower limbs and missing upper-limb and Allen test involvement.
references: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
management: Complete and permanent cessation of all tobacco and nicotine exposure is the definitive disease-modifying intervention and the single strongest determinant of limb salvage
Give intravenous prostanoids such as iloprost for critical ischaemia, ischaemic rest pain and ulceration
Provide meticulous foot and wound care, analgesia and protection from cold and trauma to the affected limbs
Manage the accompanying superficial migratory thrombophlebitis and Raynaud phenomenon
Recognise that conventional surgical revascularisation is rarely feasible because of distal, segmental disease; consider sympathectomy or intermittent pneumatic compression for refractory ischaemia
Reserve amputation for intractable gangrene or infection
Coordinate multidisciplinary vascular and intensive smoking-cessation support and escalate promptly for critical limb ischaemia
